q: can I give Motrin to my 8 month old for fever
text: Yes, ibuprofen (Motrin) can be given to a child over 6 months old — it should not be used in children younger than 6 months, according to MedlinePlus [6]. It helps reduce fever, and is usually given every 6 to 8 hours [6]. Know how much your child weighs before giving it [6]. The dose depends on the child's weight; check the packaging or leaflet to make sure the medicine is suitable for your child, or speak to a pharmacist or doctor if you're not sure [3]. You can also give paracetamol instead, but do not alternate ibuprofen and paracetamol unless a doctor or nurse tells you to [2]. Keep breastfeeding as normal and watch for signs of dehydration [3]. Get medical advice if you're worried, or if the medicine is not helping [3].

q: my son threw up twice this morning, what should I give him to drink
text:
For vomiting, the goal is to replace the fluids and electrolytes your son has lost. Oral rehydration solutions are made for children and you can buy them without a prescription, according to MedlinePlus [1]. Give small sips of rehydration solution regularly to replace lost fluids [6]. If he is on formula or solid foods, you can also give small sips of extra water [6]. Do not give young children fruit juice or fizzy drinks — they can make vomiting worse [6]. Do not make formula weaker [6]. Keep giving his usual diet in small amounts [6].

Get help if there are signs of dehydration [3].

q: how do I know if my child is getting dehydrated from vomiting
text:
Dehydration happens when the body loses more fluid than it takes in, and vomiting is one of the common causes [1]. The main risk of vomiting is dehydration, so the priority is keeping fluids going in [3].

When your child vomits, wait 20 minutes, then give oral rehydration solution — 2 to 5 ml every 5 minutes for an hour, according to the SEUP [5]. Watch how well they take it; if fluids go down well, you can slowly increase how often you offer them [5]. Don't use homemade solutions like lemonade, or commercial soft drinks [5]. Oral rehydration fluids you can buy over the counter are the most helpful for mild dehydration, and sports drinks without caffeine or alcohol can help a little, though they don't replace important nutrients and minerals, according to the CDC [2].

Get medical care if you think your child is severely dehydrated — that can need fluids through a vein in hospital [2]. Also check with your paediatrician if your child seems floppy or listless, vomits many times, or won't take fluids [3].

A cough that is worse at night is one of the main signs of asthma in children, according to MedlinePlus [6]. Asthma symptoms usually come and go, and may be worse at night and early in the morning [4].

If your child has asthma, keep using their inhaler as usual, and see your doctor if treatments are not helping, if they need their inhaler more often, or if you need advice about using it [4]. Get medical help right away if there is severe coughing, serious breathing problems, or if they turn very pale or blue in the face, lips or fingernails [6].

A cough that lingers after a cold is common: cold symptoms can last for 10 to 14 days, according to MedlinePlus [6]. Keep offering fluids and let your son rest; there is no medicine that shortens a cold.

If the cough changes — bouts of coughing that last for a few minutes and are worse at night, a "whoop" sound when gasping between coughs, thick mucus that makes him vomit, or difficulty breathing after a coughing bout — that is not a simple cold, and he should be seen, according to the NHS [4]. q: he has a cough but no fever and is eating normally
text:
A cough without a fever, with a child eating normally, is not one of the situations the guidance covers as a fever problem — fever is the body's natural response to fighting infections like coughs and colds, according to the NHS [1].

If a fever does appear, the AEPap says to first check the temperature with a thermometer, in the armpit, and if there are no warning signs start with physical measures: remove extra clothing, offer fluids, reduce physical activity and a lukewarm bath if the child is comfortable [4]. Antitérmicos are used when the temperature is above 38-38.5°C (101.3 °F) in the armpit or when the fever causes discomfort [6]. Paracetamol can be given every 4-6 hours, no more than five doses a day, and ibuprofen every 6-8 hours; the dose is calculated by weight, not age [6].

Get help if your child has other signs of illness such as a rash alongside a high temperature, has a high temperature lasting 5 days or more, does not want to eat or is not their usual self and you are worried, or is dehydrated, according to the NHS [1].

q: my daughter has red spots all over her stomach and they appeared today
text:
Red spots that appear suddenly and itch a lot are often hives, which in childhood are mostly caused by an infection rather than an allergy, according to the SEUP [3]. The spots are raised, red patches that move around — appearing in one area as they fade from another — and can come with swelling of the hands, feet, elbows or face [3].

Hives can usually be treated at home [5]. Keep your daughter comfortable, and speak to a pharmacist about antihistamine medicine to help with itching [1]. Bathing in cool water and patting the skin dry without rubbing can help, as can loose clothes [1]. Paracetamol can help with any pain or discomfort [1].

Call your local emergency number if there is swelling around her mouth or she is struggling to breathe [5].

q: my 6 year old fell from the bed and hit the back of his head
text:
Most head injuries are not serious, and most children recover quickly, according to the SEUP [2][6]. The usual symptoms are headache, confusion, brief memory loss, dizziness, nausea, vomiting and drowsiness [1].

Let him rest, physically and mentally, for 24 to 48 hours depending on how hard the knock was — no sport and no screens (tablets, video games, smartphones) during that time, then a gradual return to normal activity [4]. He can sleep, but after a more significant knock it is worth waking him every 4 hours [6]. He can eat and drink as usual, according to his appetite [6]. If he has a headache, you can give ibuprofen or paracetamol in the dose your doctor indicates [6].

Go to the emergency department if he has any of the symptoms above, or any behaviour that worries you — also if the fall was from more than one metre [5].

q: what foods should I start with for a baby who just turned 6 months
text: Start with single vegetables and fruits, according to the NHS. Try mashed or soft, cooked sticks of parsnip, broccoli, potato, yam, sweet potato, carrot, apple or pear [5]. Include vegetables that are not sweet, such as broccoli, cauliflower and spinach, to help your baby get used to a range of flavours [5]. Make sure any cooked food has cooled right down before offering it [5]. Foods containing allergens, such as peanuts, hens' eggs, gluten and fish, can be introduced from around 6 months, one at a time and in small amounts so you can spot any reaction [5]. Full-fat dairy products such as pasteurised cheese and plain yoghurt can be given from around 6 months; choose ones with no added sugar [5]. Babies do not need salt or sugar added to their food or cooking water [5]. At first, how much your baby eats matters less than getting them used to eating — they still get most of their energy and nutrients from breast milk or first infant formula [1].

q: my daughter is 13 months and still mostly drinks formula
text:
Once your child is 12 months old, formula milks are not needed, according to the NHS [2]. This includes first infant formula, follow-on formula, growing-up milks and other toddler milks [2]. Your baby can now drink pasteurised whole or semi-skimmed cows' milk [2]. Choose full-fat dairy products such as cheese, yoghurt and fromage frais, as children under 2 years old need the vitamins and extra energy found in them [2].

From 12 months, your child will be eating 3 meals a day containing a variety of different foods, including starchy food such as potatoes, bread and rice; fruit and vegetables; milk or dairy products; and protein from animal sources (meat, fish and eggs) or vegetable sources (dhal, beans, chickpeas and lentils) [2]. Your child may also need 2 healthy snacks in between meals [2]. Go for things like fresh fruits such as slices of apple and banana, or small pieces of soft, ripe, peeled pear or peach; cooked or raw vegetables such as broccoli florets, carrot sticks or cucumber sticks; pasteurised plain, unsweetened, full-fat yoghurt; sticks of cheese (choose a lower salt option); toast, pitta or chapatti fingers; and unsalted and unsweetened rice or corn cakes [2].

The World Health Organization recommends that all babies are breastfed for up to 2 years or longer [2]. You can keep breastfeeding for as long as it suits you both, but your child will need less breast milk to make room for more foods [2]. You can give your child unsweetened, calcium-fortified milk alternatives, such as soya, oat or almond drinks, from the age of 1 as their main drink as part of a healthy, balanced diet [2]. A dietitian can give you advice on milk alternatives to make sure your child is getting the nutrients they need [2]. Children under 5 years old should not be given rice drinks because of the levels of arsenic in these products [2].

q: how often should a newborn poop
text: How often a newborn poops varies from baby to baby — the rhythm and consistency of stools differs from one person to another, according to the SEUP [3]. It is not essential that a baby has a bowel movement every day [3]. What matters more is whether the stools become hard: constipation is an excessive increase in the hardness of the stool, with discomfort or incomplete emptying, and it may come with fewer bowel movements [6]. For a baby under 6 months, keep feeding as usual with breast milk or formula [3]. Constipation should be checked by your paediatrician unless it comes with: significant abdominal pain, being very down and complaining a lot, blood in the stool, or vomiting many times and not tolerating solids or liquids [3]. Never give laxatives or enemas without consulting your paediatrician [3].

q: my 4 year old wakes up coughing only when he lies down
text:
A cough that comes on mainly when your child lies down can be a sign of asthma, which often causes coughing at night or early in the morning, according to MedlinePlus [3]. Asthma symptoms usually come and go and may be worse at night and early in the morning, according to the NHS [4].

Keep the air moist — water can help ease a cough, whether your child drinks it or you add it to the air with a steamy shower or vaporizer [1]. Do not give cough medicine: children under four should not have it, and for children over four you should use caution and read labels carefully [1].

See your doctor if your child has asthma symptoms, or if symptoms are waking them up at night [4]. Get medical help right away if there is severe coughing, serious breathing problems, or your child turns very pale or blue in the face, lips or fingernails [3].

On steam, guidelines differ. The CDC suggests sitting with a young child in a bathroom with steam from a running shower to ease a cough. The NHS advises against it: with croup, do not put your child in a steamy room or get them to inhale steam, and do not let children breathe in steam from a bowl of hot water, because of the risk of scalding.

q: my son has asthma and is using albuterol more than usual
text: Using a reliever inhaler more often can mean your child's asthma is not as well controlled as it should be, according to the NHS [2]. Keep using the inhaler as your child's plan says, and make sure it is used correctly — a doctor, nurse or pharmacist can show you how [3]. If your child is having an asthma attack, sit them up straight to help their breathing and try to stay calm [4]. With a blue reliever inhaler, give 1 puff every 30 to 60 seconds until they feel better, up to a maximum of 10 puffs, shaking the inhaler between each puff and using a spacer if you have one [4]. With an AIR or MART inhaler, give 1 puff every 1 to 3 minutes, up to a maximum of 6 puffs [4]. If your child's personal asthma action plan has a different maximum dose, follow that plan [4]. Get help now if your child starts to feel worse at any time, does not feel better after the maximum dose of reliever inhaler, or does not have an inhaler [4]. If symptoms are no better after 10 minutes and help has not arrived, use the inhaler again, up to the same maximum dose [4]. After an attack, even if your child feels better, see your doctor within 2 days to discuss treatment and help prevent another attack [4]. See your doctor if your child needs their inhaler more often, treatments are not helping, or symptoms are stopping them doing usual activities or waking them at night [2].

q: she is making a strange noise when she breathes but is still smiling
text:
A strange noise when breathing can be a sign of croup, which is an inflammation of the vocal cords and windpipe that causes noisy breathing, a dry barking cough and a hoarse voice, according to MedlinePlus [3]. It often starts like a cold, and symptoms usually get worse at night and last three to five days [3]. Most viral cases are mild and can be treated at home [3].

Keep the child calm and comfortable, and offer fluids often. Croup is more common in children between six months and three years, and more frequent in autumn and winter [3].

If you are worried about your child's breathing, call your doctor straight away, according to MedlinePlus [3]. Croup can rarely become severe and interfere with breathing [3].

q: my 6 year old says his chest hurts when he takes a deep breath

Chest pain when breathing deeply can be a sign of asthma, according to the WHO. Asthma symptoms include chest tightness that makes it hard to breathe deeply, and they are often worse at night or during exercise [1]. Symptoms can also be caused by other conditions, so anyone with symptoms should talk to a healthcare provider [1].

Watch your child's general state at home, and look for difficulty breathing — ribs showing or the chest sinking in, fast breathing, getting tired when walking or running — or chest pain when breathing, according to the SEUP [2]. Go to the emergency department if their general state gets worse, if they are listless, sleepy or very irritable, or if difficulty breathing appears [2]. Chest pain or pain in the side when breathing is also a reason to go, so complications can be ruled out [5].

q: my baby had a seizure last year and has a fever today
text:
A febrile seizure can happen when a child has a high temperature, and it is not usually serious, according to the NHS [3]. A high temperature is 38C (100.4 °F) or more, and it usually returns to normal within 1 to 4 days [1].

Take their temperature with a digital thermometer in the top of the armpit, keeping the arm pressed to the side of the body and leaving it in place as long as the leaflet says [1]. If they have just had a bath or been wrapped in a blanket, wait a few minutes and try again [1].

Get medical help if your child has a seizure [3]. Call your local emergency number or go to the emergency department if your child has a seizure for the first time, has a seizure that lasts more than 5 minutes, is having difficulty breathing, has stiffness and twitching on only 1 side of their body, is more sleepy than usual for more than 1 hour after the seizure stops, or has more than 1 seizure within 24 hours [2]. Do not move your child or try to hold them in place, do not put anything in their mouth, and do not try to lower their temperature by undressing them or sponging them with cold water [5].

q: my 4 year old had a seizure when he was a baby, does that change anything now
text:
A febrile seizure can happen when a child has a high temperature, and it is not usually serious or likely to cause long-term effects, according to the NHS [2]. Children who have had one have a slightly increased chance of epilepsy later in life, but this is rare [3].

If your child has another seizure, keep them safe while you wait for medical help: check the time it starts and ends, protect their head with your hands or something soft, and remove any dangerous objects nearby [4]. After it ends, put your child in the recovery position and make sure there is nothing in their mouth or throat that might affect their breathing [4]. Do not move your child or hold them in place, do not put anything in their mouth, and do not try to lower their temperature by undressing them or sponging them with cold water [1].

Get medical help if your child has a seizure for the first time, a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes, difficulty breathing, stiffness and twitching on only one side, more sleepiness than usual for more than 1 hour afterwards, or more than one seizure within 24 hours [5].

q: my child has a sore throat and white stuff on the tonsils
text:
A sore throat with white patches on the tonsils is often tonsillitis, an infection of the tonsils that is a common childhood illness [1]. The tonsils can be red and swollen, and children may also have a high temperature, problems swallowing, a cough, a headache, earache or feel sick [1]. White patches or pus-filled spots on the tonsils can happen when symptoms are more severe [1].

To help soothe the throat, give plenty of water and cool or soft foods, keep them away from smoky places, and let them rest [6]. Ice cubes, ice lollies or hard sweets can help, but do not give young children anything small and hard to suck because of the risk of choking [6]. Children should not gargle with salty water [6].

See a doctor if the symptoms do not go away within a week, or if they keep getting throat infections [2]. q: can babies get dehydrated from breastfeeding

text:
First, do what the warning above says.

Breastfeeding does not cause dehydration — it protects against it. The danger of dehydration is greater the smaller the child is, according to the SEUP [1]. Keep breastfeeding normally, and even more often if your baby wants it [4]. If your baby has diarrhoea or vomiting, oral rehydration solution is what replaces the water and salts lost, and it comes ready-prepared [1]. If your baby is vomiting, wait 20 minutes, then give oral rehydration solution, 2–5 ml every 5 minutes for an hour, and if it is tolerated you can slowly increase how often you give it [7]. q: my daughter is 13 and started her period but has very heavy bleeding
text:
Heavy periods are common and may be normal for you, but treatment can help if they're affecting daily life, according to the NHS [3]. Signs include needing to change a pad or tampon every 1 to 2 hours, using two types of period product together, periods lasting more than 7 days, passing clots larger than about 2.5cm, bleeding through to clothes or bedding, avoiding daily activities, or feeling tired or short of breath a lot [3].

See your doctor about the bleeding. Heavy periods are a very common cause of iron deficiency anaemia, and heavy periods can be treated with medicine [2]. If a blood test shows the red blood cell count is low, iron tablets will be recommended, taken for about 6 months, and repeat blood tests may be carried out over the next few months to check the iron level is getting back to normal [5]. Untreated iron deficiency anaemia can make you more at risk of illness and infection, and may increase the risk of complications affecting the heart or lungs, such as an abnormally fast heartbeat or heart failure [6].

q: my 15 year old has acne that is getting worse
text:
Acne is a common skin condition causing spots that can range from mild to severe, and there are many treatment options and ways to manage it [5]. It usually affects the face, chest and back, and can cause oily or greasy skin, spots, large painful lumps under the skin, changes to skin colour and texture or scars, and skin that may feel hot or painful to touch [5]. Having acne can also affect mental health, causing anxiety, depression and low self-esteem [5].

Wash the skin twice a day with a gentle cleanser, remove make-up at the end of the day, use non-comedogenic skincare and make-up, and try treatments you put on the skin such as salicylic acid or benzoyl peroxide — a pharmacist can advise [1]. Do not pick or squeeze spots, as this can cause scars, and do not scrub the skin, as this can irritate it and make acne worse [1].

See a doctor if you've tried treating it yourself but it's not getting better, if there are lots of spots or the spots are deep, painful or causing scars, if there are signs of a skin infection such as hot, swollen and red skin, or if it's affecting their mental health [3].

q: my child has asthma but is not wheezing right now, should I still use albuterol

In every child with bronchospasm, treatment with salbutamol should be started, according to the SEUP [7]. Asthma symptoms can be mild or severe and can come and go over time [2], and sometimes bronchospasms begin with only a cough [7].

If a crisis is happening, give 2 to 4 puffs of salbutamol, one at a time, with a spacer (and a face mask for small children), and repeat this dose after 10-15 minutes [6]. Keep them resting and avoid vigorous exercise, and avoid smoky or polluted air [6]. If your child takes a maintenance treatment, keep giving it during the crisis [6].

Go to a health centre as soon as possible if the crisis does not ease after treatment at home, or if you have any doubt [6]. Go to an emergency department if they are very agitated or drowsy, turn blue or pale, if breathing gets worse — breathing faster and faster, ribs showing, lots of belly movement or the chest sinking in — or if they need inhalations very often, every two hours or less [7].

q: I found a lump behind my baby's ear, should I worry
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Swelling or redness behind the ear, or the ear pushed forward: it should be seen today
text:
A tender swelling behind the ear is one of the signs health workers are taught to feel for when a child has an ear problem [1]. Ear infections are very common in children, and most clear up on their own within 3 days, though symptoms can sometimes last up to a week [2].

Treat the pain: give ibuprofen or paracetamol regularly every 6-8 hours for the first 1-2 days, before the pain builds up [3]. Do not put anything in the ear to soothe it, and keep the ear dry, especially if it has been discharging [3]. If your baby is a baby, do frequent nasal washes with saline [3]. It is normal for them to have a small appetite — do not force them to eat [3]. If an antibiotic has been prescribed, follow the schedule exactly: dose, interval and duration [3].

See your doctor if your child is under 6 months, is generally unwell, has a fever of 39°C (102.2 °F) or above, has discharge from the ear, has had previous episodes of otitis, or has not improved after 48-72 hours of pain treatment [5]. Go to the emergency department if they are generally unwell, have a severe headache, are listless, drowsy or very irritable, or if the area behind the ear is red, painful or swollen, or the ear is pushed forward [5].

q: my 2 year old weighs 40 pounds, should I be worried
text:
40 lb = 18.1 kg.

A single weight on its own does not tell you whether a 2-year-old is in the healthy range — what matters is plotting weight and height together on a growth chart. The World Health Organization says every child should have their own chart so their growth can be followed properly [2]. For children under 5, overweight is a weight-for-height more than two standard deviations above the median of the WHO child growth standards, and obesity is more than three [6]. The WHO chose this cautious, step-by-step approach partly to avoid the risk of putting young children who are still growing on restrictive diets [2].

So ask your child's doctor to measure weight and height and plot them on the WHO chart, and to advise you on diet and physical activity if there is any concern [1].

text:
A dry cough can be a symptom of several respiratory viruses, and the cough can be severe and last 2 weeks or more, according to the WHO [1]. Most people recover from fever and other symptoms within a week without needing medical attention [1].

There is no specific treatment for these viral infections, and they usually clear up on their own in 1 to 2 weeks [5]. Rest and drinking fluids, like water, can help [5]. Over-the-counter cough and flu medicine should not be given to children younger than 6 years old unless a health care provider advises it [5].

Seek medical care if your child has trouble breathing or fast breathing, dehydration, a fever that lasts longer than 4 days, symptoms that last more than 10 days without getting better, or symptoms such as fever or cough that improve then return or worsen, according to the CDC [4]. This list is not all-inclusive; see a healthcare provider for any symptom that is severe or concerning [4].

q: my daughter has a wet cough but no fever
text:
A wet cough without fever is often just a cold, and the mucus can last up to a week while the cough may last longer than that, according to the SEUP [4]. Keep giving her plenty of fluids [4]. If she is a baby, you can do nasal washes before feeds and bedtime, preferably with saline solution and never tap water [4]. Keep her away from smoke and from places where people are smoking [4]. Do not use cough syrups or other cold medicines, especially if she is under 6 years old [4]. It is normal for her not to feel like eating much — do not force her [4]. Do not give honey if she is under one year old [4].

See a doctor if her general state gets worse, if she is listless, sleepy or very irritable, or if she has difficulty breathing [6].

q: my child has a cough after choking on food yesterday but seems okay now
banner: 🚨 Call 911 now or go to the emergency department. | Reason: Choking with breathing difficulty
text:
A cough that continues after a choking episode is something to have checked, and the SEUP says to go to the emergency department immediately for choking with difficulty breathing or constant vomiting or drooling [1]. While you get help, keep your child upright and calm, and do not give them anything to eat or drink [1].

Watch for any of these: pale, mottled, blue or grey colour; sudden spots on the skin or swelling of the lips or eyelids with difficulty breathing, vomiting or dizziness; not responding to you; excessive irritability or drowsiness; abnormal movements or a seizure; severe difficulty breathing — ribs pulling in, breathing very fast or pauses in breathing, or being drowsy; choking with difficulty breathing or constant vomiting or drooling; a deep wound with heavy bleeding that does not stop after pressing for 10 minutes; an open fracture; or a head injury with loss of consciousness [1].

q: my daughter fainted for a few seconds at school and feels fine now
text:
A fainting spell is a sudden, short loss of consciousness, and it usually happens when not enough blood or oxygen reaches the brain, according to the SEUP [2]. Children usually recover quickly after a period of rest, within a couple of minutes [5].

If she starts to feel unwell again, she should sit or lie down straight away — the change of position is often enough — and breathe slowly and deeply [5]. If she loses consciousness, it is better to lay her down with her legs raised and her head turned to the side so she breathes more easily [5]. When the discomfort and weakness have gone, she can get up slowly: sit first, then stand after a few minutes [5]. It also helps children who tend to faint to drink more fluids, especially during physical exercise [4].

Get emergency help if she takes more than 3-5 minutes to come round, if the faint happened during exercise, effort or while sitting, or if it came with palpitations, chest pain, jerking of the limbs or passing urine involuntarily, according to the SEUP [6].

q: my teenager fainted during soccer practice
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Fainting during exercise, or with palpitations or chest pain: get them seen in the emergency department today
text:
Fainting is a sudden, short loss of consciousness, and it usually happens when not enough blood or oxygen reaches the brain, according to the SEUP [2]. It is often triggered by heat, pain, fear, anxiety, standing still for a long time, or getting up suddenly [2]. Before fainting, a teenager may feel sick, have blurred vision, belly pain, sweating or ringing in the ears — these warning feelings can help them avoid another episode [2].

While it is happening, lay them down with their legs raised and their head turned to the side so they breathe better [6]. When the unwell feeling and weakness have gone, they can sit up slowly, then stand after a few minutes [6]. After a rest, children usually recover quickly, within a couple of minutes [6]. It helps to drink more fluids, especially during exercise [4].

Get emergency help if they are not breathing, cannot be woken within 1 minute, have not fully recovered or have trouble with speech or movement, have chest pain or a pounding, fluttering or irregular heartbeat, have seriously hurt themselves, are shaking or jerking, fainted while exercising, or fainted while lying down, according to the NHS [3]. The SEUP also says to call emergency services if they take more than 3-5 minutes to come round, and to consult urgently if the faint happened during exercise or effort, or came with palpitations, chest pain, jerking of the limbs, or wetting themselves [5].

q: my child says everything looks blurry after getting hit in the face with a ball
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Something stuck in the eye, or a blow to the eye: do not rub it or try to remove it; get it seen in the emergency department today
text:
Blurry vision after a hit to the face can be a sign of concussion, a type of brain injury that happens when a blow to the head or face makes the brain move inside the skull, according to the CDC [7]. A concussion can happen even if the child does not pass out, and symptoms can take hours or days to appear [6].

Have the child checked by a doctor or health care provider, and have someone observe them for a few days after the injury [6]. Rest is very important after a concussion because it helps the brain heal; at first, limit physical activity and activities that need a lot of concentration, such as studying, computer work or video games, then return to normal activities slowly when the doctor says it is okay [5].

Get help right away if there is neck pain, double vision, loss of consciousness, seizure or convulsion, vomiting over and over again, a headache that is severe or getting worse, or weak, tingling or burning feeling in the arms or legs [4].

text: Vomiting that stops your child keeping fluids down needs to be checked today. While you get help, keep offering small sips of water or let them suck on ice chips if they can't keep liquids down, according to MedlinePlus [7]. Carry on breastfeeding or bottle feeding, giving small feeds more often than usual, and give small sips of water between feeds if they're on formula or solid foods [3]. q: my child fell from a second story window but seems okay
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: A fall down stairs or from more than a metre, or crying that will not settle after a knock: get a doctor to see them today
text:
A knock on the head is the medical term for a blow to the head, which usually happens from a fall, an accident or during sport, according to the SEUP [1]. The most usual symptoms are headache, confusion, brief loss of memory, feeling dizzy, nausea, vomiting and drowsiness [1].

Keep them resting, physically and mentally, for 24 to 48 hours depending on how hard the knock was; during this time no sport and no screens — tablets, video games or smartphones — and then a gradual return to normal activities [5].

Go to the emergency department if they have any of those symptoms, or a behaviour or mood that worries you, and also if the child is under three months old or the fall was from more than a metre [3]. Warning signs to watch for at home are intense or worsening headache that does not improve with the usual paracetamol or ibuprofen, repeated vomiting, disorientation or confusion, irritability or being hard to wake in very small children, changes in usual behaviour, difficulty speaking or walking, and blood or clear fluid from the nose or ears [5]. Seek help immediately for a headache that worsens or does not improve, repeated vomiting or nausea, seizures, being unable to get up, dilated pupils in one or both eyes, difficulty speaking, weakness or numbness in the arms or legs, poor coordination, or growing confusion, restlessness or agitation, according to MedlinePlus [4].

q: my toddler swallowed a button battery

text: A swallowed button battery is an emergency — it can burn the oesophagus within hours, so go now. On the way, separate the child from the battery, and if something solid is visible in the mouth and you can reach it, take it out — never blindly, as that could make things worse, according to the SEUP [3]. Do not try to make the child vomit, and do not give water, milk, oil or any other food [3]. Try to work out how much was swallowed [3]. If the child does not respond normally, is not breathing well or has a bad colour, call the emergency number [3]. A child with a known or possible swallowed button battery needs to be assessed in the emergency department [6].

q: mi niño tiene asma y le cuesta un poquito respirar
banner: 🚨 Llama ahora al 911 o acude a urgencias. | Motivo: Dificultad para respirar grave (se marcan las costillas, respira muy rápido, pausas en la respiración, color azulado)
text: Las crisis asmáticas son episodios de tos, dificultad para respirar y ruidos de pecho producidos por obstrucción de los bronquios, y mejoran al administrar broncodilatadores como el salbutamol, según la SEUP [2]. Administra de 2 a 4 pulsaciones de salbutamol, aplicadas de una en una, con una cámara espaciadora y mascarilla facial si es pequeño, y repite esa dosis a los 10-15 minutos [6]. Mantenlo en reposo, sin ejercicio vigoroso, y evita ambientes con humo de tabaco o contaminación [6]. Si toma tratamiento de mantenimiento, debe seguir con él durante la crisis [6]. Si la crisis no cede tras el tratamiento en casa, o si te queda alguna duda, acude lo antes posible a un centro sanitario, sin olvidar la cámara espaciadora [6]. Debes consultar en urgencias si está muy agitado o somnoliento, si se pone morado o pálido, si la dificultad respiratoria empeora (respira cada vez más deprisa, se le marcan las costillas, mueve mucho el abdomen o se le hunde el pecho) o si necesita inhalaciones cada dos horas o menos [3].

text:
Si el bebé tiene menos de 3 meses, la fiebre necesita que lo vea un médico ese mismo día.

En un niño mayor, la fiebre después de las vacunas es una reacción esperable: la inmunogenicidad y la seguridad de las vacunas sistemáticas son, en general, similares a las de los recién nacidos a término, según la CAV-AEP [3]. En los prematuros, la norma general es mantener sin demoras las vacunas inactivadas del calendario [2].

No puedo darte una dosis: depende de la edad y el peso, que no tengo. La dosis unitaria de cada vacuna es la misma que en un recién nacido a término, y no hay fundamento para usar dosis reducidas o fraccionadas [1]. Las edades de vacunación siguen el calendario nacional de Estados Unidos.

Si el niño fue prematuro de menos de 28 semanas y pesó menos de 1500 g, tiene mayor riesgo de apnea y bradicardia en las 48-72 horas después de la vacunación, aunque estos fenómenos son transitorios [3].

¿Qué edad tiene? Con la edad afino la respuesta.

q: my 18 month old has a fever of 103 and won't take Tylenol
text:
103 °F = 39.4 °C.

A fever is usually a sign the body is fighting an infection, and most fevers in young children settle within a few days [1][5]. The main goal is your child's comfort, not bringing the number down [3].

Keep offering plenty of liquids so they stay hydrated, and don't force them to eat if they don't want to [3]. Dress them lightly and keep the room comfortably cool — don't bundle them up [3]. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) and ibuprofen both reduce fever in children; acetaminophen can be given every 4 to 6 hours, ibuprofen every 6 to 8 hours, and ibuprofen should not be used under 6 months [4]. The right amount depends on your child's weight [4]. If they won't take the Tylenol, you can try the other one instead [3][4]. Don't give aspirin to a child [4].

If the fever is very high, your health care provider may recommend an over-the-counter medicine such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen [1].

q: why does my 3 year old have a temperature of 105 degree celsius
text:
105 °F = 40.6 °C.

A temperature of 105°C is not possible on a thermometer — a high temperature in children is 38C (100.4 °F) or more, and it is very common in young children, according to the NHS [2]. It is the body's natural response to fighting infections like coughs and colds [1].

You can usually look after them at home, and the temperature should go down over 1 to 4 days [4]. Give them plenty of fluids, and if your baby is breastfed, continue to breastfeed as normal [4]. Look out for signs of dehydration, give them food if they want it, check on your child regularly including during the night, and keep them at home [4]. Give them either paracetamol or ibuprofen if they're distressed or uncomfortable — check the packaging or leaflet to make sure the medicine is suitable for your child, or speak to a pharmacist or doctor if you're not sure [4]. Do not undress your child or sponge them down to cool them, and do not cover them up in too many clothes or bedclothes [1]. Do not give aspirin to children under 16 [1].

Get medical advice if you're worried about your child, or if the paracetamol or ibuprofen is not helping [4].

q: my 14 year old says her throat hurts really bad when swallowing
text:
A sore throat that hurts when swallowing is very common and usually nothing to worry about — it normally gets better by itself within a week, according to the NHS [5]. It is usually caused by a virus, like a cold or flu [4].

To help soothe it: drink plenty of water, eat cool or soft foods, suck ice cubes, ice lollies or hard sweets, rest, and avoid smoking or smoky places [5]. She can gargle with warm salty water — half a teaspoon of salt in a glass of warm water, then spit it out, not swallow it [5].

Antibiotics are not normally needed, because they will not usually relieve symptoms or speed up recovery [7]. Get help if her sore throat does not improve after a week, or if she has a lump in her mouth or neck or a mouth ulcer lasting more than 3 weeks [7]. Ask for urgent advice now if you are worried, if she has a very high temperature or feels hot, cold or shivery, or if she has signs of dehydration such as peeing less than usual or dark, strong-smelling pee [7]. Get emergency help now if she has difficulty breathing or cannot swallow, is drooling, is making a high-pitched sound as she breathes, or has severe symptoms getting worse quickly [7].

q: why do I have a fever and chills today
text:
A fever is a sign your body is fighting an infection, and infections cause most fevers, according to MedlinePlus [2]. It is a defence mechanism, not a sign of seriousness by itself, and the most frequent cause is an ordinary infection, especially a viral one, according to the SEUP [3].

Drink enough fluids to prevent dehydration [2]. If the fever is very high, your doctor may recommend an over-the-counter medicine such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen; adults may also take aspirin, but children with fever must not [2]. Antipyretics lower the temperature but do not always bring it down completely, especially if it started very high, so the fever persisting after one is common and does not mean it is more serious [4]. Fever usually lasts between 2 and 4 days, though it can last longer without being more serious [4].

q: he has an inhaler but I dont know when to use it
text:
A reliever inhaler is used when symptoms come on, and a preventer inhaler is used every day to help prevent symptoms, according to the NHS [3]. Your care team will explain how and when to use your medicines, and this is written in your asthma action plan [6].

If he is having an asthma attack, sit him up straight and try to stay calm [1]. With a blue reliever inhaler, give 1 puff every 30 to 60 seconds until he feels better, up to a maximum of 10 puffs, shaking the inhaler between each puff and using a spacer if you have one [1]. With an AIR or MART inhaler, give 1 puff every 1 to 3 minutes, up to a maximum of 6 puffs [1]. If his personal asthma action plan has a different maximum dose, follow that [1].

Get help if he starts to feel worse at any time, does not feel better after the maximum dose, or does not have an inhaler [1]. See a doctor if treatments are not helping, he needs his inhaler more often, or you need advice about using it [2].

q: my daughter touched a hot pan and has a red patch on her finger
text:
A small burn like this can often be treated at home, according to the NHS [3]. A burn is damage to the skin caused by heat, such as a hot pan [1].

q: she feels hot but the thermometer says 98.6
text:
A temperature of 98.6°F (37°C (98.6 °F)) is around normal, according to MedlinePlus — a normal temperature varies from person to person but is usually around that [6]. A high temperature is usually considered to be 38°C (100.4 °F) or above, according to the NHS [4].

If you're not sure the reading is right, take it again with a digital thermometer in the armpit, following the manufacturer's instructions [1][3]. If your child has just had a bath, been wrapped in a blanket, been very active or been cuddling a hot water bottle, their temperature may be higher for a short time — let them cool down for a few minutes, but don't let them get cold or shivery, then take it again [1][2].

Get medical advice if your child has other signs of illness, such as a rash, as well as a high temperature, or does not want to eat or is not their usual self and you're worried [7].

q: my child may have swallowed a magnet
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Swallowed an object or something is stuck in the throat (batteries, magnets, a fish bone)
text:
A swallowed magnet needs medical assessment, and the SEUP lists swallowing an object, especially batteries or magnets, among the reasons to go to the emergency department [4]. While you are on the way, do not try to make your child vomit, do not give water, milk, oil or any other food, and if something solid is visible in the mouth and you can reach it, take it out — never blindly, as that could make things worse [2]. Try to work out how much was swallowed [2].

Once a swallowed object has passed the oesophagus and reached the stomach, most pass through the intestine in 4 or 5 days, helped by a diet rich in fibre, according to Ecimed; parents should check the stools and avoid laxatives [5]. A single magnet usually causes no problems, but swallowing several magnetic pieces can favour the formation of intestinal volvulus [5].

q: my child has a rash after having a fever, could it be from the fever
text:
If your child is under 3 months old, a fever needs a doctor the same day.

A rash that appears just as the fever drops is a recognised pattern in small children, according to the SEUP: a high fever for 3 to 4 days with no other findings, then the fever falls and a faint, widespread, non-itchy maculopapular rash appears and lasts 48 hours [2]. It is diagnosed by this sequence of events and the child's age, and there is no vaccine to prevent it [2].

Give paracetamol or ibuprofen if the fever is causing discomfort — paracetamol is the first choice [5]. The dose depends on your child's age and weight, so follow the dose your doctor or the leaflet gives.

Go to the emergency department if your child is limp, barely responsive or very irritable, has difficulty breathing, has skin spots that do not fade when pressed, cannot keep down solids or liquids, or is under 2 months old or immunocompromised [1].

q: what are the side effects of chickenpox shot
text: Most side effects of the chickenpox vaccine are mild and do not last long, according to the NHS [2]. They can include swelling or pain where the injection was given, a high temperature, and a rash in the area where the injection was given or more widespread — it usually develops within 1 month of vaccination [2]. More serious side effects, such as a severe allergic reaction, are very rare [2]. The person who vaccinates your child will be trained to deal with allergic reactions and treat them immediately [2].

Get an urgent appointment with your doctor if you're worried about your baby or think they might be ill [7].

q: my 10 month old is pulling his ear and crying a lot
text:
Ear infections are the most common reason parents bring their child to a doctor, and three out of four children will have at least one by their third birthday [1]. In babies who cannot yet say their ear hurts, signs to look for include tugging at the ears, crying more than usual, fluid draining from the ear, trouble sleeping, balance difficulties and hearing problems [1]. Ear infections often get better on their own within 3 days, although symptoms can sometimes last up to a week [3].

Treat the pain: give ibuprofen or paracetamol regularly every 6-8 hours for the first 1-2 days, before the pain appears, according to the SEUP [6]. Do not put anything in the ear to soothe the pain, and keep the ear dry, especially if it has been discharging [6]. If your child is a baby, do frequent nasal washes with saline [6]. If an antibiotic has been prescribed, follow the schedule correctly — dose, interval and duration [6].

Your doctor can diagnose an ear infection by looking inside the ear with an otoscope [1]. Severe infections and infections in young babies may need antibiotics [1].

q: my 3 year old keeps vomiting every time he drinks water
text:
Small sips of water or sucking on ice chips can help when it is hard to keep liquids down, according to MedlinePlus [1]. Give small amounts more often than usual, and regular small sips of rehydration solution to replace lost fluids — your pharmacist can recommend one [3]. Keep giving his usual diet, and do not give fruit juice or fizzy drinks, as they can make vomiting worse [3][6]. Vomiting usually stops in 1 or 2 days [6].

Get help if he vomits a lot and cannot keep down solids or liquids, or vomits even when he takes nothing; if the vomit is greenish, contains blood or looks like coffee grounds; if he is drowsy, limp, very thirsty, has sunken eyes, cries without tears or passes little urine; or if he has severe tummy pain or a headache [2].

q: my toddler has very hard poop and cries when he goes
text:
Hard, painful poops are constipation: fewer than three bowel movements a week, with stool that can be hard and dry, and sometimes painful to pass, according to MedlinePlus [3]. It is the increased hardness of the stool with discomfort when passing it, and it can come with tummy pain, bloating, or a feeling of not having finished [4][2]. In most cases it lasts a short time and is not serious [3].

Offer more liquids, preferably water, to soften the poops and make them easier to pass, and more meals with fibre — wholegrain cereals and bread, fruit and vegetables; don't replace fruit with juice, which has little fibre [1]. Laxatives only if your doctor says so [3][1].

See your doctor if there is blood in the stool, bad tummy pain, if he is very down and complaining a lot, or if he vomits many times and can't keep down solids or liquids [1].

q: my baby has been vomiting for six hours but still wants to breastfeed
text:
Keep breastfeeding — offer the breast normally, and even more often if your baby wants it, according to the SEUP [2]. Don't stop feeding: there's no need to fast, and food should be given in smaller amounts and more often, respecting your baby's appetite [2]. For a baby, you can use the milk they usually take, breast milk or formula [3]. Avoid fizzy drinks and sugary juices at any age, and avoid chocolate, sweets, very fatty or fried foods and sauces [3]. The symptoms usually settle on their own in less than a week [3].

Get help if your baby is under 3 months and has vomited two or more feeds; if they vomit a lot, can't keep down solids or liquids, or vomit even when they take nothing; if the vomit is greenish, contains blood or looks like brown coffee grounds; if they are drowsy, limp, very thirsty, have sunken eyes, cry without tears or pass little urine; or if they have severe tummy pain or a headache [4].

A fever in a baby is a temperature of 100.4 °F (38 °C (100.4 °F)) or more, according to the NHS [3]. A normal temperature varies a little from child to child [3]. Babies this young need to be checked by a doctor the same day, so take your baby now and keep them close while you travel [1][2].

q: my son passed out after standing in the sun for a long time
banner: 🚨 Call 911 now or go to the emergency department. | Reason: Not responding to stimuli
text:
Fainting after long time in the sun can be a sign of heat illness, and heatstroke is a life-threatening illness in which body temperature may rise above 106 °F (41 °C (105.8 °F)) in minutes, according to MedlinePlus [2].

While you wait for help, wrap your child in a cool, wet sheet, or fan them or sponge them down with cold water, according to the NHS [6]. If they lose consciousness while you're waiting for help, put them in the recovery position and tell the ambulance service, and check their breathing and pulse and carry out CPR if they show no sign of life [6].

Get help immediately if there are signs of heatstroke, including still being unwell after 30 minutes of resting in a cool place, being cooled and drinking fluids, a very high temperature, hot skin that's not sweating and might look red, a fast heartbeat, fast breathing or shortness of breath, confusion and lack of coordination, a seizure or fit, or loss of consciousness [4].

q: my toddler is struggling to breathe and the ribs are pulling in
banner: 🚨 Call 911 now or go to the emergency department. | Reason: Severe breathing difficulty (ribs pulling in, very fast breathing, pauses in breathing, blue colour)
text: A toddler who is struggling to breathe with the ribs pulling in has severe difficulty breathing, and this needs immediate care [1]. While you get help, keep your child upright and calm, and do not put anything in their mouth [1]. q: my 6 year old has a cough that is worse at night
text:
A cough that is worse at night is common in several childhood illnesses. Croup causes a barking cough, a hoarse voice and noisy breathing, and its symptoms are usually worse at night, lasting about three to five days, according to MedlinePlus [6]. Asthma also causes coughing that is worse at night or early in the morning [5]. Whooping cough brings coughing bouts that are worse at night and can last for weeks [4].

Most cases of viral croup are mild and can be treated at home [6]. If you think your child may have croup, ask your doctor for an urgent appointment — they may give medicine to shorten the illness [3].

Get medical help right away if your child has severe coughing, serious breathing problems, or turns very pale or blue in the face, lips or fingernails [5]. Also seek help if your child is getting worse or not getting better after seeing a doctor [3].

q: my 2 year old fell off the sofa and was sick once
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Vomiting after a head injury
text:
First, do what the warning above says.

A knock on the head is the medical term for a blow to the head, which usually happens from a fall, an accident or during sport, and the usual symptoms include headache, confusion, brief loss of memory, dizziness, nausea, vomiting and drowsiness, according to the SEUP [1].

Keep your child resting, both physically and mentally, for 24 to 48 hours depending on how hard the blow was; during this time no sport and no screens — tablets, video games or smartphones — and then a gradual return to normal activities [5]. Watch them over the first 24 hours after the knock for signs of seriousness [2].

Get help straight away if there is worsening headache that does not improve, repeated vomiting or nausea, seizures, inability to get up, dilated pupils in one or both eyes, difficulty speaking, weakness or numbness of the arms or legs, poor coordination, or growing confusion, restlessness or agitation, according to MedlinePlus [4]. Also go if there is intense, progressive headache that does not improve with the usual paracetamol or ibuprofen, repeated vomiting, disorientation or confusion, irritability or difficulty waking in very small children, changes in usual behaviour, difficulty speaking or walking, or blood or clear fluid from the nose or ears [5].

q: my child keeps scratching red patches on his arms
text:
Itchy red patches on the arms are common in children and are often a sign of eczema, a skin condition that most often starts in babies and young children, according to the NHS [1]. Scratching can make the skin turn red and swell and itch even more [2].

Keep nails short, and put anti-scratch mittens on babies to limit damage from scratching [5]. Apply moisturising treatments (emollients) to the skin as often as possible, at least twice a day, and keep moisturising even if the eczema improves [5]. Wash with an emollient instead of soap, avoid things that make it worse such as soap, washing detergent, some fabrics or pets, and keep your child cool, because being hot makes eczema more itchy [5].

See your doctor if your child has symptoms of atopic eczema, or if treatments are not helping [4]. Ask for an urgent appointment if the skin is blistered, crusty, leaking fluid or has spots filled with pus; if it is painful, swollen or feels warm; if it suddenly gets worse or gets bigger; or if your child has a high temperature or feels generally unwell [4].

text:
Wheezing after running around is a common pattern: symptoms often start after physical effort, and in preschool children the main cause of wheezing is viral respiratory infections, according to the SEUP [2][7]. Earache after a cold is often an infection of the middle ear, behind the eardrum. It usually happens as a complication of an upper respiratory cold with a lot of nasal mucus, according to the SEUP [5].

q: my baby has a blocked nose and cant feed properly
text:
A blocked nose and trouble feeding are common with a cold: sneezing, a stuffy nose, runny nose, sore throat and cough usually start a few days after infection, and some symptoms can last 10 to 14 days, according to MedlinePlus [2].

Keep the nose clear with nasal washes, and feed in small, frequent amounts to keep feeding and hydration good [1]. Hold your baby in a semi-upright position to help them breathe, give fever medicine if there is fever, keep them strictly away from tobacco smoke, and wash your hands often to avoid passing the virus on [1].

q: my 5 year old complains of stomach ache and won't eat anything
text:
A stomach ache with no appetite is often part of a tummy bug: norovirus causes vomiting, diarrhoea, tummy pain, headache and body aches, and usually gets better in about 2 days, according to the NHS [4]. The CDC says symptoms usually appear 12 to 48 hours after exposure, and the most common ones are diarrhoea, vomiting, nausea and stomach pain [5].

Offer drinks in small sips often, and let your child rest. If they are not eating much for a day or two, that is common with a tummy bug.

Constipation can also cause stomach ache, bloating and feeling sick — it's likely if your child has not had a poo at least 3 times in the last week, if the poo is large or small, dry, hard or lumpy, if they strain or are in pain when they poo, or if they feel they haven't fully emptied their bowels [6].

See your doctor if the stomach ache keeps going, if your child seems unwell in themselves, or if they are not drinking.

q: my baby is 4 months and has a fever of 38
text:
A fever is the body's natural response to fighting infections like coughs and colds, according to the NHS [7]. It is usually something you can look after at home, and the temperature should go down over 1 to 4 days [1].

Do give them plenty of fluids – if your baby is breastfed, continue to breastfeed as normal [1]. Look out for signs of dehydration, check on your child regularly including during the night, and keep them at home [1]. You can give them either paracetamol or ibuprofen if they're distressed or uncomfortable – check the packaging or leaflet to make sure the medicine is suitable for your child, or speak to a pharmacist or doctor if you're not sure [1]. Do not give ibuprofen to a child who is under 3 months, weighs under 5kg, has chickenpox, or is dehydrated [7]. Do not give aspirin to children under 16 years of age [7]. Do not undress your child or sponge them down to cool them, and do not cover them up in too many clothes or bedclothes [7].

Get medical advice if you're worried about your child, or if the paracetamol or ibuprofen is not helping [1]. Call your local emergency number if your child has a stiff neck, has a rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it, is bothered by light, has a fit for the first time, has unusually cold hands and feet, has changes to their skin colour such as blue, grey, paler than usual or blotchy skin, or blue, grey or paler than usual lips or tongue, is drowsy and hard to wake, is extremely agitated or is confused, has difficulty breathing, breathlessness or breathing very fast, or is not responding like they normally do, or is not interested in feeding or normal activities [7].

q: my daughter has mosquito bites all over her legs, what can I put
text:
Most insect bites are harmless, though they sometimes cause discomfort, and mosquito bites usually itch [6]. The bite should get better in a few days [1].

Put an ice pack wrapped in a cloth, or a clean cloth soaked in cold water, on the bites for at least 20 minutes, and keep the area raised if it's swollen [1]. You can give painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen if they're painful, use antihistamines to relieve itching, and use a hydrocortisone cream to reduce itching and swelling [1]. Do not let her scratch the bites, as they could get infected, and do not use home remedies such as bicarbonate of soda [7].

See a pharmacist if the skin around a bite feels hot or looks red, it's painful, the area looks swollen, or there's pus or fluid coming out [7]. Ask for an urgent appointment or get help from your local emergency number if symptoms get worse or are not getting better, or if she has a high temperature and swollen glands [7].

q: मेरे बच्चे को कल से दस्त हो रहे हैं और वह खाना नहीं खा रहा
text:
दस्त का इलाज मौखिक पुनर्जलीकरण घोल (ORS) से किया जाना चाहिए, और साथ ही ज़िंक की 10–14 दिन की पूरक खुराक दस्त की अवधि कम करती है और नतीजे बेहतर बनाती है, विश्व स्वास्थ्य संगठन के अनुसार [3]। ORS साफ पानी, नमक और चीनी का मिश्रण है, जो छोटी आंत में सोखा जाता है और मल के साथ निकले पानी और इलेक्ट्रोलाइट्स की भरपाई करता है [1]। ज़िंक की पूरक खुराक दस्त के एक दौर की अवधि 25% तक घटा देती है [1]।

अभी यह करें: बच्चे को ORS घोल पिलाते रहें [1]। खाना खाने से इनकार करने पर भी पोषक तत्वों से भरपूर आहार — जिसमें माँ का दूध भी शामिल है — दस्त के दौरान देना जारी रखें, क्योंकि इससे कुपोषण और दस्त का चक्र टूटता है [1]।

डॉक्टर से सलाह लें, खासकर लगातार बने रहने वाले दस्त के इलाज के लिए, या जब मल में खून हो या निर्जलीकरण के लक्षण दिखें, विश्व स्वास्थ्य संगठन के अनुसार [1]।

[3] WHO — "Diarrhoeal disease", section "Overview", p. 1 — https://www.who.int/news-room/f

q: मेरे बच्चे को बुखार के साथ लाल दाने निकल आए हैं
text:
अगर बच्चा 3 महीने से छोटा है, तो बुखार में उसी दिन डॉक्टर को दिखाना ज़रूरी है।

बुखार के साथ लाल दाने कई चीज़ों से हो सकते हैं। हैंड, फुट एंड माउथ डिज़ीज़ में पहले गले में दर्द, तेज़ बुखार और खाने का मन न करना होता है, और कुछ दिन बाद मुँह में छाले तथा हाथ-पैरों पर, कभी-कभी ग्रोइन और नितंबों पर, उभरे हुए लाल दाने निकल आते हैं; ये लक्षण आमतौर पर हल्के होते हैं, ऐसा NHS कहता है [3]। यह बीमारी आमतौर पर 7 से 10 दिन में खुद ठीक हो जाती है और इसे ठीक करने की कोई दवा नहीं है [1]। लक्षणों में मदद के लिए ठंडे तरल पदार्थ पिलाएँ ताकि मुँह को आराम मिले और पानी की कमी न हो, पर खट्टे पेय जैसे फलों का रस न दें; दही जैसा नरम खाना दें और गरम, नमकीन व मसालेदार खाना न दें [1]। दर्द के लिए पैरासिटामोल या आइबुप्रोफेन दी जा सकती है, पर खुराक बच्चे की उम्र और वज़न पर निर्भर करती है [1]। मुँह के छालों के लिए फार्मासिस्ट से जेल, स्प्रे या माउथवॉश के बारे में पूछें; वे बता देंगे कि बच्चों के लिए कौन-से ठीक हैं [1]।

अगर दाने चेहरे या गर्दन पर निकलकर पूरे शरीर पर फैल रहे हैं, तो यह खसरा हो सकता है — ऐसे में डॉक्टर से बात करें [1]।

बच्चे की उम्र कितनी है? उम्र जानकर मैं जवाब और सटीक कर सकता हूँ।

q: मेरा 6 महीने का बच्चा दूध कम पी रहा है और पेशाब भी कम कर रहा है
banner: 🚨 इन लक्षणों के साथ बच्चे को आज ही इमरजेंसी में दिखाना चाहिए, देर न करें। | कारण: पानी की कमी के लक्षण: आँखें धँसी, कम पेशाब, सूखा मुँह, लगातार उल्टी या 24 घंटे से ज़्यादा दस्त
text:
सबसे पहले, ऊपर की चेतावनी में जो लिखा है वह कीजिए।

मेडलाइनप्लस के अनुसार, पेशाब का कम आना या पेशाब का गाढ़ा होना और बदबू आना इस बात का संकेत हो सकता है कि बच्चा पर्याप्त तरल नहीं पी रहा है [3]। एनएचएस के अनुसार, बच्चे को पर्याप्त तरल, खासकर पानी, पिलाएँ ताकि वह दिन में नियमित रूप से पेशाब करे और प्यासा न लगे [4]। एसईयूपी के अनुसार, मुँह से पुनर्जलीकरण घोल (ओआरएस) थोड़ी-थोड़ी मात्रा में बार-बार दें, और घर के बने घोल या कोल्ड ड्रिंक्स इस्तेमाल न करें [1]। स्तनपान सामान्य रूप से, और अगर बच्चा माँगे तो उससे भी अधिक बार जारी रखें [8]। दस्त या उल्टी की दवा बिना बाल रोग विशेषज्ञ से पूछे न दें [1]।

q: मेरी बेटी बिस्तर से गिर गई और उसके बाद एक बार उल्टी हुई
banner: 🚨 इन लक्षणों के साथ बच्चे को आज ही इमरजेंसी में दिखाना चाहिए, देर न करें। | कारण: सिर पर चोट के बाद उल्टी
text:
सबसे पहले, ऊपर की चेतावनी में जो लिखा है वह कीजिए।

सिर की चोट के बाद उल्टी होना एक ऐसा लक्षण है जिस पर घर पर नज़र रखनी चाहिए, और SEUP के मुताबिक बार-बार उल्टी होना मतलब हालत बिगड़ने का संकेत हो सकता है [1]। चोट के बाद 24 से 48 घंटे तक शारीरिक और मानसिक आराम ज़रूरी है — इस दौरान खेल-कूद और मोबाइल, टैबलेट या वीडियो गेम जैसी चीज़ें नहीं [1]। इसके बाद धीरे-धीरे सामान्य गतिविधियों में लौटना चाहिए [1]।

घर पर इन बातों पर ध्यान दें: तेज़ या बढ़ता हुआ सिरदर्द जो आम दवा (पैरासिटामोल या इबुप्रोफेन) से ठीक न हो, बार-बार उल्टी, भ्रम या दिशा-भूलना — बहुत छोटे बच्चों में चिड़चिड़ापन या जगाने में मुश्किल, व्यवहार में बदलाव, बोलने या चलने में दिक्कत, और नाक या कान से खून या साफ़ तरल निकलना [1]।
sources: [1] SEUP — "Traumatismo craneal. Información para padres" (2025), section "¿CUÁNDO PUEDE V

नाक या कान से खून या साफ़ तरल निकलने का पूरा संकेत (पैसेज में अधूरा है)

q: बच्चे को कब्ज है और पॉटी करते समय बहुत रोता है
text:
कब्ज़ में पॉटी करते समय बच्चे का रोना आम बात है — रोने के सामान्य कारणों में कब्ज़ भी शामिल है, ऐसा NHS कहता है [2]।

अभी के लिए: बच्चे को आराम पहुँचाने की कोशिश करें और रोना शांत होने का इंतज़ार करें [1]। अगर पता न चले कि परेशानी क्या है, तो अपने डॉक्टर से बात करें या स्वास्थ्य कर्मी से पूछें [2]।

डॉक्टर से संपर्क करें अगर बच्चा लगातार रो रहा है और आप उसे चुप नहीं करा पा रहे, या उसका रोना उसके सामान्य रोने जैसा नहीं लग रहा, या उसमें बीमारी के संकेत हैं जैसे तेज़ बुखार या दूध पीने में दिलचस्पी न हो [4]। तुरंत मदद लें अगर बच्चे को दौरा पड़े, त्वचा-होंठ-जीभ नीले, स्लेटी, पीले या धब्बेदार दिखें, वह बेजान या सुस्त हो या आसानी से न जागे, साँस लेने में तकलीफ़ हो, बहुत ज़्यादा उल्टी हो, तापमान बहुत ज़्यादा या बहुत कम हो, दबाने पर न मिटने वाले दाने हों, या पिछले 8 घंटे में पेशाब की नैप्पी गीली न हुई हो [4]। अपनी अंतर्ज्ञान पर भरोसा करें [4]।

q: मेरे बच्चे के हाथ पैर ठंडे हैं लेकिन शरीर गर्म है
text:
जब बुखार चढ़ रहा होता है तो बच्चे का ठंड लगना, कंपकंपी आना और हाथ-पैरों का ठंडा होना सामान्य है — त्वचा पर जाल जैसा धब्बेदार रूप भी दिख सकता है, खासकर हाथों और पैरों पर। बुखार उतरते समय बच्चा पसीना-पसीना हो जाएगा, लाल हो जाएगा और उसे गर्मी लगेगी, ऐसा SEUP कहता है [1]।

बुखार आमतौर पर 2 से 4 दिन रहता है, हालांकि कुछ दिन ज़्यादा भी रह सकता है और इससे ज़्यादा गंभीरता नहीं जुड़ती। दवा से तापमान कम होता है, पर हमेशा पूरी तरह नहीं उतरता — खासकर अगर बुखार बहुत तेज़ हो; इसलिए दवा के बाद भी बुखार बना रहना आम है और इसका मतलब ज़्यादा गंभीर होना नहीं है [2]। बुखार शरीर की रक्षा का तरीका है, अपने आप में गंभीरता की निशानी नहीं [5]। बुखार में पानी की कमी से बचने के लिए पर्याप्त तरल देना ज़रूरी है [4]।

घर पर बच्चे की सामान्य हालत और रंग पर नज़र रखें, और त्वचा पर ऐसे लाल धब्बे दिखें जो दबाने पर गायब न हों तो ध्यान दें [2]। आपातकालीन सेवा में तुरंत जाएं अगर बच्चा सुस्त, कम प्रतिक्रिया देने वाला या बहुत चिड़चिड़ा हो; सांस लेने में तकलीफ हो; त्वचा पर दबाने से न मिटने वाले धब्बे हों; मुंह से ठोस या तरल कुछ भी न ले पा रहा हो; या बच्चा 2 महीने से छोटा हो या प्रतिरक्षा-दबाव वाला हो, ऐसा SEUP कहता है [7]।

q: मेरा बच्चा बहुत सुस्त है और ठीक से जाग नहीं रहा
banner: 🚨 अभी 112 पर कॉल करें या तुरंत इमरजेंसी ले जाएँ। | कारण: जवाब नहीं दे रहा; बहुत ज़्यादा सुस्ती या चिड़चिड़ापन
text:
बच्चे का सुस्त हो जाना और ज़्यादा देर जागते न रहना निमोनिया की गंभीरता के संकेतों में गिना जाता है, विकासपीडिया के अनुसार [2]। ऐसे में तुरंत वैद्यकीय सहायता लेनी चाहिए [2]।

जब तक मदद मिले, बच्चे को अपने पास रखें और उसका खाना-पीना चालू रखने की कोशिश करें [2]। बुखार उतारने के लिए गुनगुने पानी में कपड़ा भिगोकर पूरा शरीर पोंछें, सिर्फ माथा नहीं [2]।

अस्पताल ले जाते समय इन बातों का ध्यान रखें: बुखार से दौरे पड़ना, बच्चे का खाने-पीने या स्तनपान को राजी न होना, साँस लेते समय पसलियों का अंदर खिंचना, सीने से कराहने या सींटी जैसी आवाज़ आना, और त्वचा, होंठ, नाखून या चेहरे पर नीली झलक दिखना — इनमें से कोई भी लक्षण दिखते ही तुरंत वैद्यकीय सहायता लेनी चाहिए [2]।
sources: [2] Vikaspedia — "बच्चों को होने वाली आम बीमारियॉं — स्रोत: भारत स्वास्थ्य" (2020), sectio

q: मेरे बच्चे ने आज बहुत कम पेशाब किया है
banner: 🚨 इन लक्षणों के साथ बच्चे को आज ही इमरजेंसी में दिखाना चाहिए, देर न करें। | कारण: पानी की कमी के लक्षण: आँखें धँसी, कम पेशाब, सूखा मुँह, लगातार उल्टी या 24 घंटे से ज़्यादा दस्त
text:
बहुत कम पेशाब आना निर्जलीकरण का संकेत हो सकता है, और प्यास बहुत लगना, बिना आँसू के रोना या आँखें धँसी दिखना भी इसी ओर इशारा करते हैं, SEUP के अनुसार [1]।

अब ओरल रीहाइड्रेशन सॉल्यूशन (ORS) थोड़ी-थोड़ी मात्रा में बार-बार दें — तैयार मिलने वाला घोल इस्तेमाल करें, घर के बने घोल या कोल्ड ड्रिंक न दें [1]। बच्चा जितना तरल खो रहा है, उतना ही पी सके, यह ध्यान रखें [1]। दस्त या उल्टी की दवा बिना बाल रोग विशेषज्ञ से पूछे न दें [1]। खाना बंद करने की ज़रूरत नहीं; सामान्य खाना थोड़ी-थोड़ी मात्रा में, बार-बार दें, और बच्चे की भूख का सम्मान करें [8]। चिकनी चीज़ें, मिठाई और जूस से बचें; दूध और स्तनपान सामान्य रूप से जारी रखें, माँगे तो और बार [8]। स्पोर्ट्स ड्रिंक न दें [8]।

डॉक्टर से तुरंत मिलें अगर बच्चा बहुत उल्टी करे, ठोस या तरल कुछ भी न रख पाए, बिना कुछ पिए भी उल्टी करे, या उल्टी हरी हो, उसमें खून हो या कॉफ़ी जैसी भूरी दिखे [8]।
sources: [1] SEUP — "Gastroenteritis aguda. Información para padres" (2025), section "Ofrecer en pe
[8] SEUP — "Gastroenteritis aguda. Información para padres" (2025), section "¿DEBEMOS OFRE

missing: मार्की चेतावनी संकेत जो तुरंत आपातकालीन देखभाल की मांग करते हैं: सुस्ती, उत्तरदायित्व में कमी, या गंभीर चिड़चिड़ापन [1]
लगातार या तीव्र पेट दर्द या बहुत खून वाला दस्त [1]
बच्चा जितना तरल खो रहा है उतना पी नहीं पा रहा है (बहुत बार और बहुत अधिक पतला दस्त) [1]
छोटे बच्चों में निर्जलीकरण का खतरा अधिक होता है [1]
util.note: La respuesta es útil pero omite señales de alarma graves (somnolencia, irritabilidad marcada, dolor abdominal intenso o sangre en heces) que el pasaje pide vigilar.

q: मेरी बेटी को तेज बुखार और बैंगनी जैसे दाग हो गए हैं
banner: 🚨 अभी 112 पर कॉल करें या तुरंत इमरजेंसी ले जाएँ। | कारण: दबाने पर न मिटने वाले दाने (सेप्सिस या मेनिन्जाइटिस का शक)
text:
अगर बच्चा 3 महीने से छोटा है, तो बुखार में उसी दिन डॉक्टर को दिखाना ज़रूरी है।

तेज़ बुखार बच्चों में बहुत आम है और आमतौर पर 1 से 4 दिनों में तापमान सामान्य हो जाता है, एनएचएस के अनुसार [3]। त्वचा पर ऐसे दाग जो दबाने पर भी न मिटें, तो तुरंत मदद लेनी चाहिए — एसईयूपी कहती है कि ऐसे दाग होने पर आपातकालीन सेवा में जाना चाहिए [1]।

जब तक मदद मिले: बच्चे को बहुत ज़्यादा कपड़ों या रज़ाई में न लपेटें, और उसे ठंडा करने के लिए कपड़े न उतारें या स्पंज न करें — तेज़ तापमान संक्रमण के खिलाफ शरीर की स्वाभाविक प्रतिक्रिया है, एनएचएस के अनुसार [2]। 16 साल से छोटे बच्चे को एस्पिरिन न दें, और डॉक्टर या नर्स के कहे बिना आइबुप्रोफेन और पैरासिटामोल बारी-बारी न दें [2]। दवा की मात्रा बच्चे की उम्र और वज़न पर निर्भर करती है, इसलिए वह डॉक्टर या दवा के पर्चे के अनुसार ही दें।

एसईयूपी के अनुसार, अगर बच्चा सुस्त या कम प्रतिक्रिया देने वाला या बहुत चिड़चिड़ा हो, सांस लेने में तकलीफ हो, दबाने पर न मिटने वाले दाग हों, मुँह से कुछ भी न ले पाए, या बच्चा 2 महीने से छोटा हो या प्रतिरक्षा कमज़ोर हो, तो आपातकालीन सेवा में जाएँ [1]।
sources: [1] SEUP — "Fiebre. Información para padres" (2025), section "¿CUÁNDO DEBEMOS CONSULTAR EN
[2] NHS — "High temperature (fever) in children" (2025), section "Don’t", p. 1 — https://w
[3] NHS — "High temperature (fever) in children" (2025), section "High temperature (fever)

missing: बुखार के साथ दाने और सुस्ती/कम प्रतिक्रिया जैसे लक्षणों के संयोजन में तुरंत आपातकालीन सेवा (112) पर कॉल करने की सलाह स्पष्ट रूप से नहीं दी गई।
बच्चे की उम्र या वजन के अनुसार बुखार की सीमा (जैसे 3 महीने से कम उम्र में 38°C या अधिक) का जिक्र नहीं किया गया।

q: mere 3 saal ke bacche ko bukhar 102 hai, paracetamol kitna du
text: Paracetamol bukhar aur bechaini mein madad karta hai, aur aap ise dawai ki dukaan se khareed sakte hain [4]. AEPap ke mutabiq, dawa ki matra bachche ke wazan se nikali jati hai, umar se nahi — isliye apne bachche ka wazan jaan lijiye [3]. Paracetamol har 4-6 ghante mein diya ja sakta hai, aur din mein paanch se zyada baar nahi [3]. Dawa ki sahi matra ke liye PediBot ka dose calculator istemal kijiye, ya apne doctor se poochhiye [3]. AEPap kehta hai ki agar bachche ko bukhar ke saath bechaini ho ya woh risk group mein ho to dawa dene ka intezar na karein [3]. Agar aapne bachche ko packet ya leaflet par likhi matra se zyada paracetamol de diya hai, to turant medical salah lijiye, kyunki ye kabhi-kabhi khatarnak ho sakta hai [7].
sources: [3] AEPap — "Antitérmicos (para la fiebre)", section "¿Cuándo utilizar los antitérmicos?",
[4] NHS — "Paracetamol for children (Calpol) - Other common brands: Panadol" (2025), secti
[7] NHS — "Paracetamol for children (Calpol) - Other common brands: Panadol" (2025), secti

missing: Passage [3] says paracetamol can be used when axillary temperature is above 38-38.5°C or when fever causes discomfort — the answer does not state this threshold.
Passage [3] says paracetamol must not be given to a child weighing less than 3 kg.
Passage [3] says the danger of paracetamol is liver damage.
Passage [5] says if the child vomits within 10-15 minutes of a dose, the dose may be repeated.
gap: The exact paracetamol dose in ml or mg for a 3-year-old of a given weight is not in the passages.
Whether 102°F (about 38.9°C) needs medicine at all, and how to measure temperature correctly, is only partly covered.

q: mera baby raat ko bahut khans raha hai
text:
Raat mein khansi hona kai cheezon mein se ek lakshan ho sakta hai. MedlinePlus ke mutabik bachchon mein asthma ke lakshanon mein khansi shaamil hai, khaaskar raat ko ya subah jaldi [1]. SEUP ke mutabik asthma ke daure mein bachchon ko raat ko khansi, saans ki kami aur ghabrahat ho sakti hai [3].

Ghar par aaram karayein, khoob saara taraL peeyein, saaf humidifier ya thande bhaap wala vaporizer istemaal karein, aur saline naak ki boondein ya spray dein [6]. SEUP ke mutabik khansi ke syrup, mucolytics, corticoide ya respiratory physiotherapy faydemand nahi hain [2]. Kisi bhi dawa se pehle apne doctor se poochein [6].

Turant medical madad lein agar saans lene mein sakht dikkat ho, khansi lagataar ho, bolne mein dikkat ho, ya honton ke aas-paas neela rang dikhe [3].
sources: [1] MedlinePlus — "Asma en niños", section "¿Cuáles son los síntomas del asma en los niños
[2] SEUP — "Bronquiolitis. Información para padres" (2025), section "¿PUEDE PREVENIRSE?",
[3] SEUP — "Crisis asmática. Información para padres" (2025), section "¿CUÁLES SON LOS SÍN
[6] MedlinePlus — "Resfrío", section "¿Cuáles son los tratamientos para el resfrío común?"

wrong: Answer attributes to SEUP [2] the statement that cough syrups, mucolytics, corticoids or respiratory physiotherapy are not useful, but passage [2] is about bronchiolitis, not about night cough in general; applying it here is a different situation.

Answer says 'SEUP ke mutabik asthma ke daure mein bachchon ko raat ko khansi, saans ki kami aur ghabrahat ho sakti hai' — passage [3] mentions nocturnal cough, breathlessness and choking sensation, but not 'ghabrahat' (agitation); this is a misstatement.
missing: Passage [1] lists other asthma symptoms in children: chest tightness, rapid breathing, wheezing, tiredness, dark circles under eyes, irritability, difficulty feeding/sucking in babies.
Passage [1] says asthma attacks can be gradual or sudden and can sometimes be life-threatening.
Passage [3] mentions chest indrawing, rib and clavicle retractions (tiraje) and faster breathing as signs to watch.
Passage [6] warns that children and adolescents should not take aspirin, and that some cold/cough medicines contain ingredients not recommended for children or duplicate analgesics.
gap: No passage covers what to do for a baby with night cough when asthma is not suspected and there are no red flags (e.g., how long to wait, when to see a doctor).
No passage covers the possibility of whooping cough, croup, or other causes of night cough in a baby.
No passage gives guidance on safe sleeping position or home environment for a baby with night cough.

q: mere bete ke pairon par lal dane hain aur khujli ho rahi hai
text: Chhote, ubhre hue lal dane jo khujli karte hain, aksar heat rash (prickly heat) hote hain — yeh takleef deta hai par aam taur par harmless hota hai aur kuch dinon mein khud theek ho jata hai, NHS ke mutabiq [6]. Sabse zaroori hai skin ko thanda rakhna taaki pasina aakar rash ko na chidhaye: dheele cotton kapde pehnao, halki rajai use karo, thande paani se nahi ya shower karao, aur dehydration se bachne ke liye khoob paani pilao [6]. Khujli ya chubhan shaant karne ke liye thandi cheez — geele kapde ya ice pack (towel mein lipti hui) — 20 minute tak lagao, aur khujlane ke bajaye rash ko thapthapao ya sehlayo; khushbudar shower gel ya cream mat lagao [6]. Agar saans lene mein dikkat ho ya munh ke aas-paas sujan ho to turant emergency help lein, NHS ke mutabiq [5].
sources: [5] NHS — "Rashes in babies and children" (2024), section "Raised, itchy spots or patches"
[6] NHS — "Heat rash (prickly heat)" (2024), section "Heat rash (prickly heat)", p. 1 — ht

Heat rash ek doosre insaan ko nahi lagta (passage 4/6)
Agar yakeen na ho ke heat rash hai to 'other rashes in babies and children' dekhein (passage 6)

q: mera bachcha bed se gir gaya aur ek baar ulti ki
banner: 🚨 इन लक्षणों के साथ बच्चे को आज ही इमरजेंसी में दिखाना चाहिए, देर न करें। | कारण: सिर पर चोट के बाद उल्टी
text:
सबसे पहले, ऊपर की चेतावनी में जो लिखा है वह कीजिए।

Bed se girne ke baad ek baar ulti hona — SEUP ke mutabik, sar par chot lagne ke baad ulti aana ek aisa lakshan hai jise doctor ko dikhana chahiye [1]. Ghar par 24 se 48 ghante tak sharirik aur mansik aaram karein, khel-kood aur mobile, tablet ya video games bilkul na karein [1]. Aaram ke baad normal kaam dhire-dhire shuru karein [1].

Raste mein bachche ko ulti ke liye baithne ya karwat par lita dein, taaki saans na ruke. Kuch bhi muh mein na dein.

In lakshanon par turant dhyan dein: tez ya badhta sar dard jo aam dawa se theek na ho, baar-baar ulti, behoshi ya confusion, bahut chhote bachchon mein chidchidapan ya jagaana mushkil, vyavhaar mein badlav, bolne ya chalne mein dikkat, naak ya kaan se khoon ya saaf paani [1].
sources: [1] SEUP — "Traumatismo craneal. Información para padres" (2025), section "¿CUÁNDO PUEDE V

missing: बार-बार उल्टी होने पर तुरंत इमरजेंसी जाना (पैसेज 1 में 'vómitos repetidos' एक चेतावनी संकेत है)
बच्चे को होश में रखने और बार-बार जगाने की सलाह — bahut chhote bachchon mein jagaana mushkil hona khatre ka sanket hai
सिर की चोट के बाद 24-48 घंटे निगरानी रखना और अकेले न छोड़ना
gap: भारत में सिर की चोट के लिए कौन सा आपातकालीन नंबर (108/112) मिलाएं — किसी पैसेज में नहीं है
बच्चे की उम्र के हिसाब से कब घर पर रखें और कब अस्पताल जाएं — पैसेज में उम्र-आधारित मार्गदर्शन नहीं है
util.note: जवाब सही दिशा में है, लेकिन बार-बार उल्टी और होश में रखने जैसे ज़रूरी चेतावनी संकेत छूट गए हैं।

q: mere bacche ko kabz hai aur potty karte waqt rota hai
text:
Mere bachche ko kabz hai aur potty karte waqt rota hai — yeh aam baat hai, kyunki constipation un kai kaaranon mein se ek hai jinki wajah se bachche rote hain, NHS ke mutabik [3].

Agar bachcha breastfeeding kar raha hai, to positioning aur attachment sudhaarne se unhe shaant hone mein madad mil sakti hai; iske liye aap breastfeeding group ya apne health visitor se madad le sakte hain [5]. Agar bachcha constant rota hai aur aap use chup kara nahi paate, ya uski rone ki awaaz aam jaisi nahi lagti, to yeh bimaari ka sanket ho sakta hai — agar use tez bukhaar hai ya doodh peene mein dilchaspi nahi hai to apne doctor se milen [7].

Turant madad len agar bachche ko daura (seizure) aata hai, honth ya skin neeli, grey, pale ya blotchy ho jaati hai, woh responsive nahi hai ya aaram se nahi jaagta, saans lene mein dikkat hai, bahut zyada ulti ho rahi hai, temperature bahut zyada ya bahut kam hai, aisi rash hai jo dabane par bhi nahi jaati, ya pichhle 8 ghante mein peshaab nahi kiya [7].
sources: [3] NHS — "Colic" (2022), section "Symptoms of colic", p. 1 — https://www.nhs.uk/condition

q: my 2 year old has bad cough at night not sleeping
text:
A cough that is worse at night is common in whooping cough: after about a week of cold-like symptoms, children get coughing bouts that last for a few minutes and are worse at night, according to the NHS [3]. The cough may last for several weeks or months [3]. Coughing fits that get worse and happen more often, especially at night, can go on for up to 10 weeks or more, and recovery is slow, according to MedlinePlus [4].

Ask a pharmacist about cough syrup or cough medicine — some cough medicines should not be given to children under 12 years old — and these will not stop the cough but may help them cough less [1].

Ask for an urgent appointment or get help from your local emergency number if the cough is very bad or quickly gets worse, they feel very unwell, have chest pain, the side of their neck feels swollen and painful, they find it hard to breathe, or they are coughing up blood [1].
